entries.title: Salvage, Outposts, and Derelicts
entries.subtitle: Every abandoned place has already defeated at least one plan.
entries.summary: Guides boarding, evidence preservation, survivor handling, contamination, salvage rights, and withdrawal.
body: An abandoned submarine or station should be treated as an unresolved incident scene. The original hazard may remain active, and later hazards may have arrived. Power may be intermittent, doors may be compromised, atmosphere may be unsafe, and survivors may be injured, infected, armed, deceptive, or simply terrified.

Boarding teams must separate rescue, reconnaissance, security, and salvage priorities. Stripping a site before confirming survivors, hazards, and ownership creates both moral and operational complications.
Withdrawal criteria should be established before entry. A team already deep inside a structure will redefine 'too dangerous' until no safe route remains.
doctrine: Rescue and hazard control precede discretionary salvage.
Mark searched spaces and unsafe routes.
Preserve logs, bodies, damage patterns, and unusual biological evidence when investigation matters.

procedures.title: Initial boarding
steps: Confirm docking or return route.
Test atmosphere and power state.
Establish a secure entry compartment.
Search for survivors and active hazards.
Report before splitting the team or opening sealed spaces.

procedures.title: Withdrawal decision
steps: Compare oxygen, ammunition, injuries, route integrity, and hostile activity against the pre-set limit.
Take portable evidence and critical recovered items.
Do not delay for low-value cargo.
Seal or mark hazards when possible and report what remains.

warnings: The most valuable object in a derelict is often the explanation for why it became one.
fieldNotes: A sealed door is not an invitation. It is a statement awaiting translation.

entries.title: Hostile Boarding and Internal Security
entries.subtitle: Defend the boat without destroying the boat.
entries.summary: Sets priorities for contact reports, compartment control, crew identification, detention, sabotage response, and recovery.
body: Internal combat collapses the distinction between battlefield and life-support system. Every firefight occurs beside wiring, pipes, oxygen, medical stores, pressure doors, and crew members moving toward unrelated emergencies.

Security must establish where the threat is, which compartments remain secure, how noncombatants will move, and who controls each firing direction. Locking every door may trap the crew with the attacker; opening every door may remove the only defensible boundaries.

Sabotage indicators require preservation as well as response. Repeated failures, missing tools, altered wiring, contaminated supplies, disabled alarms, forged orders, and unexplained access should be documented before routine repair erases the pattern.
doctrine: Identify friend, threat, and background before engagement.
Control routes rather than chasing blindly.
Detain when safe; do not abandon immediate survival tasks to conduct punishment.

procedures.title: Boarding response
steps: Announce contact, compartment, number, and direction of movement.
Secure command, reactor, medical, armory, and diving access.
Move unarmed crew behind controlled boundaries.
Assign firing sectors and casualty access.
Sweep and reopen compartments deliberately.

procedures.title: Suspected saboteur
steps: Protect critical controls and supplies.
Separate the suspect from access without unnecessary violence.
Record observed actions, times, and witnesses.
Inspect affected systems for secondary devices or delayed failures.
Transfer custody and evidence to command.

warnings: A locked armory is useful only when the correct people can still reach it.
fieldNotes: Security that cannot explain what happened has contained a person, not necessarily the threat.

entries.title: Depth Psychology and Crew Strain
entries.subtitle: The mind also operates under pressure.
entries.summary: Describes isolation, fatigue, fatalism, ritual behavior, conflict escalation, and practical intervention.
body: Life beneath Europa narrows the world to machinery, duty schedules, recycled air, repeated corridors, distant settlements, and the knowledge that the environment outside can kill without warning. People respond with professionalism, humor, superstition, ritual, aggression, withdrawal, and sometimes belief systems that promise meaning where ordinary life offers only maintenance.

Not every strange habit is illness, and not every calm crew member is well. Watch for sudden sleep disruption, reckless indifference, fixation on the ocean, escalating pranks, concealed self-harm, compulsive risk-taking, paranoia, inappropriate laughter during casualty response, and refusal to remove contaminated clothing or equipment.

Intervention should be practical: rest, food, medical evaluation, relief from watch, clear expectations, private conversation, and removal from dangerous access when necessary. Public humiliation produces concealment, not recovery.
doctrine: Fatigue is a system fault with a human interface.
Take sudden personality change seriously after injury, hypoxia, medication, infection exposure, or prolonged stress.
Humor may preserve morale; humiliation and hazard creation do not.

procedures.title: Concerned crew intervention
steps: Speak privately and describe observed changes.
Check immediate safety, injury, sleep, medication, and exposure.
Notify medical or command when risk exceeds peer support.
Adjust access to weapons, diving, reactor, or isolated duty when necessary.
Document significant events without turning rumor into diagnosis.

warnings: A person can be both joking and in danger.
fieldNotes: The crew member who stops caring whether the boat survives is already participating in the next failure.

entries.title: The Assistant and the Clown Question
entries.subtitle: Useful work is a role. Useless disruption is a choice.
entries.summary: Separates harmless crew culture from neglect, obstruction, impersonation, theft, and dangerous pranks.
body: Assistants are often assigned where the crew has the greatest need and the least patience. A competent assistant becomes the connective tissue between departments: carrying supplies, learning repairs, moving casualties, relaying information, cleaning hazards, and noticing unattended tasks. An incompetent assistant becomes mobile clutter. The distinction is training and conduct, not title.

Clowning, costumes, musical intrusion, grease paint, jokes, and ritual nonsense can relieve stress in an environment designed to produce it. The Primer does not prohibit absurdity. It prohibits using absurdity as an excuse to steal equipment, impersonate command, obstruct access, contaminate workspaces, disable systems, drug shipmates, conceal explosives, or escalate a prank after the first person stops laughing.

The question is never whether the act was funny to the person performing it. The question is whether it consumed emergency capacity, endangered another crew member, damaged trust, or forced the crew to treat a joke as a possible attack.
doctrine: Assistants should be given explicit tasks, tools, and a reporting point.
Costume does not remove professional obligations.
A prank ends immediately when it interferes with safety, consent, access, command, or truthful reporting.

procedures.title: Evaluating a prank
steps: Did it alter a critical system, medicine, weapon, pressure boundary, alarm, identification method, or emergency route?
Did it deprive someone of equipment or consent?
Could a reasonable crew member mistake it for sabotage, infection, hostile boarding, or command action?
Did the performer stop when ordered?
If any answer is unsafe, treat the incident as misconduct rather than entertainment.

warnings: Never grease a pressure-suit seal, medical instrument, weapon grip, ladder, hatch control, or person who has told you to stop.
fieldNotes: The clown may honk. The clown may not become the alarm system.

footnotes.title: On the two organized responses to the deep
footnotes.text: The Children of the Honkmother and the Church of the Husk are not interchangeable expressions of eccentricity. Both offer a disturbing view of how people seek identity and certainty under extreme isolation, but one commonly externalizes strain through performance, disruption, and escalating prank culture while the other embraces secrecy, bodily transformation, and voluntary union with a lethal parasite. See Section XIX for the full comparative caution.

entries.title: The Two Calls Below the Ice
entries.subtitle: One promises laughter against the dark. The other promises that the dark can enter you.
entries.summary: Provides the Primer's detailed caution regarding the Children of the Honkmother and the Church of the Husk.
body: Among Europan crews, two organized movements repeatedly appear wherever isolation, deprivation, fear, and distrust of ordinary institutions become severe: the Children of the Honkmother and the Church of the Husk. They are opposed in style and often in membership, yet both convert the psychological pressure of life beneath the ice into a total explanation of suffering.

The Children of the Honkmother are commonly regarded by working submariners as obnoxious, disruptive, and more interested in grease paint, jokes, honking bicorns, and theatrical disorder than useful labor. That judgment is often earned when pranks escalate into theft, false alarms, system tampering, drugging, obstruction, or humiliation. Their public absurdity can create genuine solidarity, but it can also provide concealment for people who enjoy forcing others to treat danger as entertainment.

The Church of the Husk is more secretive and more directly lethal. Its adherents may seek voluntary infection by the husk parasite, interpreting loss of ordinary humanity as transcendence, adaptation, communion, or liberation from fear. The organism they revere is associated with catastrophic outbreaks, murdered crews, and hollowed bodies turned against the living. A profession built upon preventing infection cannot treat deliberate infection as private belief.

These movements also flourish where material institutions fail. Supply collapse, long routes, damaged stations, weak medical access, and political abandonment create populations ready to believe that the established order has offered neither dignity nor survival. Coalition rebuilding, industrial recovery, and secure logistics reduce the conditions in which cults recruit, but coercion without material improvement merely confirms their account of a hostile system. Jovian Separatists and other opposition groups may exploit the same grievances without sharing either cult's theology.

The Primer's position is practical. Belief alone is not grounds for abuse. Hazardous conduct is grounds for intervention. Honking is not infection. A costume is not sabotage. A prayer is not a breach. But system tampering, coercion, concealed exposure, deliberate infection, theft of medical supplies, and recruitment through threats must be treated according to the danger they create.
doctrine: Judge conduct, access, exposure, and evidence—not clothing alone.
Do not allow fear of cult activity to become permission for collective punishment.
Deliberate infection, concealed exposure, and parasite distribution are immediate biosecurity threats.
Disruptive pranks that imitate emergencies or sabotage are security incidents regardless of claimed religious meaning.

procedures.title: Suspected Honkmother-linked hazard
steps: Separate harmless expression from the specific dangerous act.
Restore stolen, altered, or obstructed equipment.
Identify witnesses and preserve evidence of tampering.
Use ordinary discipline unless evidence supports organized sabotage or coercion.

procedures.title: Suspected Husk-linked cell
steps: Notify medical, security, and command.
Protect diagnostic supplies, antidotes, diving access, ventilation routes, and weapons.
Isolate exposed personnel using humane biosecurity procedures.
Search for parasite material, deliberate transmission equipment, and coerced recruits.
Document contacts and symptoms before moving the vessel or population.

warnings: Do not conduct a parasite examination with an audience of armed amateurs.
fieldNotes: The desire to understand a cult does not require granting it access to the ballast tank.

footnotes.title: Institutional caution
footnotes.text: A starving station does not become stable because its residents were lectured more firmly. Security operations that ignore food, medicine, power, work, and reliable transport may suppress symptoms while preserving recruitment conditions.

entries.title: The Emergency Priority Ladder
entries.subtitle: When everything is failing, choose the failure that removes your ability to answer the others.
entries.summary: Provides a common decision framework for simultaneous flooding, fire, power loss, casualties, hostile contact, and navigation danger.
body: Real submarine emergencies do not wait their turn. The crew may face flooding, fire, electrical loss, an unconscious medic, hostile contact, and unsafe terrain at once. The priority ladder prevents each department from treating its own problem as the entire world.

The ladder is not rigid. A small fire beside ammunition may outrank a large flood in an isolated ballast space. A navigation hazard may require immediate movement even while repairs are incomplete. The governing question is which condition will soonest cause irreversible loss of life or remove the ability to control the remaining conditions.
Command must continually restate the current priority, assign owners to secondary threats, and revise the order as conditions change.
doctrine: Immediate mass-casualty threat.
Loss of pressure integrity or breathable atmosphere.
Uncontrolled fire, reactor, electrical, or explosive hazard.
Loss of buoyancy, propulsion control, or collision avoidance.
Active hostile threat preventing recovery.
Critical casualties whose treatment cannot safely wait.
Secondary repairs, inventory recovery, evidence collection, and comfort systems.

procedures.title: Sixty-second stabilization cycle
steps: Name the greatest immediate threat.
Assign one responsible person or team.
Name the next two threats and assign containment.
Confirm communications and escape routes.
Reassess after any major change or every sixty seconds during rapid escalation.

warnings: Do not send every available person to the loudest compartment.
fieldNotes: The highest priority is the problem that will soon decide all other priorities for you.

entries.title: Incident Reports, Lessons, and the Crew's Memory
entries.subtitle: A crew that records only heroism will repeat every preventable mistake.
entries.summary: Defines after-action reporting, evidence preservation, corrective action, and memorial responsibility.
body: An incident report is not a punishment document. It is the vessel's external memory: what happened, what was known, what actions were taken, what failed, what worked, and what must change before the same sequence returns.

Reports should distinguish observation from inference. 'The junction box was open and wet' is observation. 'The engineer sabotaged it' is an allegation requiring evidence. Times, locations, alarms, orders, medication, ammunition, system states, and witness accounts should be recorded before memory becomes a negotiation.

Lessons must produce action. A recommendation without an owner, deadline, or verification method is a polite form of forgetting. Corrective work may include repair, redesign, training, supply changes, access control, watch changes, or amendment of the Primer itself.
Dead and missing crew members should be named accurately. Their loss should not be reduced to a joke, rumor, or convenient story that protects the surviving chain of command.
doctrine: Preserve facts before assigning motive.
Record near misses as well as casualties.
Assign and verify corrective actions.
Amend doctrine when repeated experience proves it incomplete.

procedures.title: Minimum incident record
steps: Date, voyage, vessel, location, and watch.
Initial condition and first report.
Timeline of alarms, orders, system changes, injuries, treatments, and weapons use.
Contributing conditions and failed safeguards.
Corrective actions, responsible owner, and verification date.

procedures.title: Crew debrief
steps: Stabilize medical and operational needs first.
Hear involved departments separately before group reconstruction.
Identify both successful actions and preventable failures.
Protect truthful reporting from retaliation.
Publish the lessons needed by future watches.

warnings: Do not use 'operator error' as a substitute for explaining the conditions that made the error easy and the safeguards that failed to catch it.
fieldNotes: The ocean keeps no records for you.
